Explanation: Each enzyme or enzyme complex requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP). These connect thiamine deficiency to carbohydrate metabolism, the pentose phosphate pathway, and branched-chain amino acid breakdown.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: B1-dependent enzymes; TPP-requiring enzymes
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin B1, PDF p. 133
Notes: TPP is the shared cofactor. PDH and BCKDH are multienzyme complexes requiring five cofactors (TPP, lipoate, FAD, NAD+, CoA); transketolase requires only TPP. Board overlap: keep separate from PLX-BCH-032 (B-vitamin cofactor precursors).

Explanation: All four coagulation factors require vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation for calcium binding and effective coagulation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors; Gamma-carboxylated clotting factors
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin K, PDF p. 130
Notes: Proteins C and S also undergo vitamin K-dependent carboxylation but are anticoagulants, not clotting factors; key the answer to vitamin K, not merely clotting factors.

Explanation: The renal (and intestinal) dibasic amino acid transporter defect in cystinuria impairs reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA). Cystine accumulation in urine produces characteristic stones.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: COLA amino acids; Amino acids with impaired reabsorption in cystinuria
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Cystinuria and Organic Acidemias, PDF p. 109
Notes: Cystine is the disulfide dimer of cysteine; keep distinct from cysteine. Do not label as dibasic amino acids only, since cystine is a disulfide-linked dimer. Board overlap with PLX-BCH-052 (cystinuria diagnostics) - do not co-place.

Explanation: Pyruvate can be converted to these products by pyruvate dehydrogenase, pyruvate carboxylase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alanine aminotransferase, respectively.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Products formed from pyruvate; Pyruvate conversion products
Source Section: Energy Production > Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex, PDF p. 36
Notes: Acetyl-CoA formation via PDH is irreversible; do not accept reversible pyruvate conversions as an alternate name.

Explanation: These enzymes provide the bypass reactions around the irreversible glycolytic steps. Pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase together bypass pyruvate kinase.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Enzymes bypassing irreversible glycolysis; Gluconeogenic bypass enzymes
Source Section: Carbohydrates > Gluconeogenesis, PDF p. 43
Notes: Specify fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, not the regulatory fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase.

Explanation: These sites have low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase. During hyperglycemia, trapped sorbitol contributes to osmotic injury.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Sites of diabetic polyol-pathway injury; Sites with limited sorbitol dehydrogenase
Source Section: Carbohydrates > Sorbitol and the Polyol Pathway, PDF p. 46
Notes: Mixed organ-level (kidney) and cell-level (Schwann cell) labels follow the source. Sorbitol is one contributor to - not the sole cause of - diabetic complications. Competing category: targets of diabetic microvascular/neuropathic complications.

Explanation: These four are the fibril-forming collagens providing mechanical strength, in contrast to network-forming type IV and anchoring type VII.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Fibril-forming collagens; Mechanical-strength fibrillar collagens
Source Section: Connective Tissue > Introduction to Collagen, PDF p. 24
Notes: Do not accept all collagen types, which omits the fibrillar distinction.

Explanation: These four vitamins depend on intact intestinal lipid absorption for dietary uptake and can be deficient in fat malabsorption.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: ADEK; Vitamins absorbed with dietary fat
Source Section: Vitamins > Introduction to Vitamins, PDF p. 127; Lipid Metabolism > Lipid Digestion and Absorption, PDF p. 83
Notes: Dietary absorption dependence does not exclude endogenous vitamin D synthesis or bacterial vitamin K production.

Explanation: These agents reach the CNS via dynein-mediated retrograde transport along axonal microtubules. For tetanus the transported agent is the toxin, not the intact bacterium.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Dynein-associated neural transport; Agents traveling retrogradely in axons
Source Section: Cell Biology > Cytoskeleton, PDF p. 8
Notes: REVISED: Tile 1 Clostridium tetani replaced with Tetanus toxin and title changed from Pathogens to Agents - the toxin, not the intact bacterium, undergoes retrograde axonal transport (Yen and Thwaites, Lancet 2019). Poliovirus and rabies travel via motor neurons; HSV via sensory neurons (Ludlow et al., Acta Neuropathol 2016). Original source names the organism.

Explanation: These medications disrupt microtubule function, affecting intracellular transport or mitosis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Microtubule-targeting drugs; Tubulin-directed medications
Source Section: Cell Biology > Cytoskeleton, PDF p. 8
Notes: Mechanisms and clinical uses differ; do not claim all four stabilize microtubules or are chemotherapeutics. Competing category: mitotic-spindle inhibitors.

Explanation: Copper is a required cofactor for each, linking it to oxidative phosphorylation, pigment formation, connective-tissue cross-linking, and cytosolic antioxidant defense.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Copper-dependent enzymes; Copper-containing enzymes
Source Section: Vitamins > Trace Elements, PDF p. 140; Connective Tissue > Menkes Disease, PDF p. 28
Notes: REVISED: Tile 4 narrowed from Superoxide dismutase to Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1) - copper is the catalytic metal of SOD1/SOD3, whereas mitochondrial SOD2 is Mn-dependent (Lutsenko et al., Physiol Rev 2025). Board warning: do not co-place a Mn-SOD tile.

Explanation: These enzymes use NADPH as reducing power in glutathione regeneration, cholesterol synthesis, fatty acid synthesis, and the phagocyte oxidative burst, respectively.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: NADPH-consuming enzymes; Enzymes using NADPH reducing power
Source Section: Oxidative Stress > Pentose Phosphate Pathway and Respiratory Burst, PDF pp. 59-60
Notes: NADPH oxidase generates ROS rather than detoxifying them; antioxidant enzymes fails as an alternate. Avoid additional interchangeable NADPH-user tiles on one board.

Explanation: Folate or B12 deficiency and MTHFR deficiency impair homocysteine remethylation; CBS deficiency impairs transsulfuration. Each can raise homocysteine.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hyperhomocysteinemia causes; Impaired homocysteine clearance
Source Section: One-Carbon Metabolism > Homocysteine Metabolism and Homocystinuria, PDF pp. 54-55
Notes: MMA and methionine distinguish the defects (B12 raises MMA; CBS raises methionine). Avoid additional homocysteine-elevating tiles on the same board.

Connection Title: Inherited defects that impair urea-cycle ammonia disposal
Explanation: Each inherited defect impairs ammonia disposal through the urea-cycle system. NAGS deficiency acts by reduced activation of CPS I rather than loss of a cycle enzyme.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Inherited urea-cycle disorders; Genetic defects of urea-cycle ammonia detoxification
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Disorders of the Urea Cycle, PDF p. 114
Notes: Ambiguity re-scored 2->1: all four are recognized urea cycle disorders causing hyperammonemia (Ah Mew and Lichter-Konecki, Paediatr Drugs 2025). Retain qualifiers - NAGS activates CPS1 (regulatory, not a core cycle enzyme); arginase deficiency gives a progressive spastic course with less prominent neonatal hyperammonemia. Inheritance differs (OTC X-linked; others autosomal recessive). Do not describe a uniform severe neonatal presentation.

Connection Title: Glycogen storage diseases with hepatic involvement
Connection Type: Shared tissue involvement within a disease family
Explanation: GSD types I, III, IV, and VI are the hepatic-involvement group. Their defects involve glucose release, debranching, branching, and hepatic glycogen phosphorylase, respectively.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hepatic glycogen storage disorders; GSD types I, III, IV, and VI
Source Section: Glycogen > Overview of Glycogen Storage Diseases, PDF p. 69; disease sections, PDF pp. 70, 72-73, 75
Notes: Cori (III) and Andersen (IV) can also involve muscle and overlap PLX-BCH-040 (muscle group) - do not co-place both categories on one board. Do not accept liver-only GSDs or uniform early fasting hypoglycemia.

Explanation: Vitamin B6 as PLP supports the decarboxylation step in synthesis of all four. Serotonin synthesis requires hydroxylation before decarboxylation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PLP-dependent neurotransmitter synthesis; Neurotransmitter products of B6-requiring decarboxylases
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin B6, PDF p. 136; Protein Metabolism > Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, and Charged Amino Acid Metabolism, PDF pp. 105, 107-108
Notes: Do not claim all four are monoamines, or that tryptophan converts to serotonin in one step. Board overlap with PLX-BCH-072 (PLP enzymes - uses enzyme tiles, not products).

Explanation: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation, producing the characteristic hair, bleeding, and healing abnormalities.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Vitamin C deficiency findings; Impaired collagen hydroxylation manifestations
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin C, PDF p. 132; Connective Tissue > Collagen Synthesis, PDF p. 25
Notes: Individual findings are not exclusive to scurvy. Competing category: general collagen dysfunction (less specific given corkscrew hairs/perifollicular hemorrhage).

Explanation: Deficient functional type I collagen affects bone, sclera, dentin, and the ossicles/inner ear, producing these findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Brittle bone disease findings; Type I collagen disorder manifestations
Source Section: Connective Tissue > Osteogenesis Imperfecta, PDF p. 26
Notes: Hearing loss is not universal and varies with age and subtype; do not require all four findings in every patient.

Explanation: This neurovisceral and urinary constellation occurs during AIP attacks associated with accumulation of ALA and porphobilinogen.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: AIP neurovisceral attack findings; Acute intermittent porphyria manifestations
Source Section: Porphyrias > Acute Intermittent Porphyria, PDF p. 122
Notes: Urine color is variable. Lead toxicity covers the first three but is distinguished by lack of the urine change. AIP is non-blistering; do not imply photosensitivity.

Connection Title: Susceptibility factors for porphyria cutanea tarda
Explanation: These exposures/conditions are associated with symptomatic porphyria cutanea tarda - susceptibility associations, not sufficient causes on their own.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PCT susceptibility factors; Factors associated with symptomatic porphyria cutanea tarda
Source Section: Porphyrias > Heme Synthesis and Porphyria Cutanea Tarda, PDF pp. 120, 123
Notes: Smoking appears on p. 120, not the shorter p. 123 list; both pages cited. Distinguish susceptibility from the UV-triggered skin injury that produces lesions.

Connection Type: Shared structural class and diagnostic role
Explanation: These intermediate filament proteins mark epithelial, mesenchymal, muscle, and glial differentiation, respectively.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Intermediate filament immunohistochemistry markers; Lineage-associated intermediate filaments
Source Section: Cell Biology > Cytoskeleton, PDF p. 8
Notes: GFAP = glial fibrillary acidic protein. Expression is not universally tumor-specific; do not infer a diagnosis from one stain. Competing category: tumor lineage markers.

Connection Title: Findings associated with primary ciliary dyskinesia
Explanation: Dysfunctional motile cilia impair airway clearance and sperm motility; abnormal embryonic nodal cilia can disrupt organ laterality.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Motile cilia dysfunction findings; Primary ciliary dyskinesia manifestations
Source Section: Cell Biology > Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, PDF p. 9
Notes: Situs inversus (~50%) and infertility are not universal. Do not label this four-item set the Kartagener triad. Competing category: Kartagener syndrome (situs-inversus subset).

Explanation: Failure to tag lysosomal enzymes with mannose-6-phosphate causes extracellular enzyme elevation and intracellular inclusions. Urinary GAGs are normal or only mildly elevated, helping distinguish I-cell disease from the mucopolysaccharidoses.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Mucolipidosis II clues; Failed lysosomal enzyme targeting findings
Source Section: Cell Biology > I-Cell Disease, PDF p. 4
Notes: REVISED: Tile 3 Normal urinalysis replaced with Normal/near-normal urinary glycosaminoglycans - the actual discriminator from MPS. GAGs do accumulate in ML II/III, but urinary GAG excretion is typically normal or only mildly elevated versus the marked elevation in MPS (Cusmano-Ozog et al., CAP/ACMG, Genet Med Open 2024). Competing category: Hurler syndrome (shares coarse features).

Explanation: Deficient hexosaminidase A allows GM2 storage, producing characteristic retinal and lysosomal findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tay-Sachs diagnostic associations; Hexosaminidase A deficiency clues
Source Section: Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Tay-Sachs Disease, PDF p. 14
Notes: No hepatosplenomegaly, distinguishing from Niemann-Pick. Competing category: other GM2 gangliosidoses (distinguished by HexA deficiency).

Explanation: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency affects skin, sweating, peripheral nerves, and kidneys, producing this characteristic combination.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Fabry manifestations; Clinical effects of alpha-galactosidase A deficiency
Source Section: Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Fabry Disease, PDF p. 15
Notes: Renal failure is a later complication; do not imply it accompanies every early presentation. X-linked.

Explanation: Glucocerebroside storage in macrophages and involvement of bone, liver, and spleen explain these associations.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Gaucher clinical and histologic clues; Glucocerebrosidase deficiency associations
Source Section: Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Gaucher Disease, PDF p. 18
Notes: Prefer the named histologic tile (crumpled-tissue-paper macrophages) over generic bone pain. Competing category: sickle cell disease (matches clinical findings but lacks Gaucher cells).

Explanation: Deficient galactocerebrosidase leads to psychosine accumulation and characteristic globoid cells, with optic atrophy among the neurologic findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Globoid cell leukodystrophy clues; Krabbe diagnostic findings
Source Section: Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Krabbe Disease, PDF p. 17
Notes: Optic atrophy is a possible manifestation, not mandatory in every patient.

Explanation: Deficient arylsulfatase A prevents sulfatide breakdown; storage causes demyelination and metachromatic staining of macrophage vacuoles.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Metachromatic leukodystrophy clues; Arylsulfatase A deficiency findings
Source Section: Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, PDF p. 16
Notes: Low enzyme activity alone is not sufficient standalone clinical verification.

Explanation: Classical EDS combines joint and skin extensibility with tissue fragility, abnormal scarring, and poor healing.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Classical EDS manifestations; Classical Ehlers-Danlos clinical features
Source Section: Connective Tissue > Ehlers Danlos Syndrome, PDF p. 27
Notes: Do not treat the four findings as universal across all EDS subtypes. Competing category: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (broader).

Connection Type: Shared disease presentation and laboratory pattern
Explanation: Impaired copper export from enterocytes (ATP7A) causes systemic copper deficiency, with characteristic hair and pigmentation changes and low circulating copper and ceruloplasmin.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Menkes diagnostic pattern; ATP7A-related copper deficiency findings
Source Section: Connective Tissue > Menkes Disease, PDF p. 28
Notes: Low ceruloplasmin also occurs in Wilson disease and cannot identify Menkes by itself. Competing category: systemic copper deficiency.

Explanation: Defective fibrillin (FBN1) produces the skeletal, ocular, and aortic manifestations of Marfan syndrome.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Marfan clinical findings; FBN1-associated manifestations
Source Section: Connective Tissue > Elastin, Fibrillin, and Marfan Syndrome, PDF p. 29
Notes: Upward (superior) lens displacement contrasts with downward displacement in homocystinuria. Aortic dissection is a possible complication, not required for diagnosis.

Connection Title: B vitamins supplying PDH and alpha-KGDH cofactors
Explanation: These vitamins supply TPP, FAD, NAD+, and CoA for both the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes; lipoic acid is the additional nonvitamin cofactor.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Vitamin precursors for PDH cofactors; B vitamins required by alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Source Section: Energy Production > Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex and TCA Cycle, PDF pp. 36-37
Notes: The vitamin tiles are precursors, not the activated cofactors; do not omit lipoic acid when teaching the full five-cofactor list. Board overlap with PLX-BCH-001.

Explanation: These carbon sources enter gluconeogenesis through pyruvate, DHAP, or TCA intermediates.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Gluconeogenic substrates; Carbon inputs to new glucose production
Source Section: Carbohydrates > Gluconeogenesis, PDF p. 43; Lipid Metabolism > Fed vs. Fasting State, PDF p. 96
Notes: Propionyl-CoA contributes via methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA (TCA), not a one-step conversion to glucose. Keep other glucogenic amino acids off the same board unless disambiguated.

Connection Title: Hormones that increase PEPCK in the source
Explanation: These four hormones increase PEP carboxykinase per the source, supporting increased glucose production.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hormonal upregulators of PEP carboxykinase; Hormones promoting PEPCK-mediated gluconeogenesis
Source Section: Carbohydrates > Gluconeogenesis, PDF p. 43
Notes: Do not imply identical receptor pathways, direct allosteric activation, or identical regulatory timescales. Competing category: hormones promoting gluconeogenesis.

Connection Title: Amino acids whose catabolism yields propionyl-CoA
Explanation: These amino acids are catabolized to propionyl-CoA, which feeds the methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA pathway.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Propionyl-CoA-producing amino acids; Amino acid inputs to the propionyl-CoA pathway
Source Section: One-Carbon Metabolism > Homocysteine Metabolism, PDF p. 54; Protein Metabolism > Branched Chain Amino Acids, PDF p. 110
Notes: Isoleucine also yields acetyl-CoA; this category does not assert exclusive glucogenic metabolism. All four are essential amino acids, but that broader category is weaker. Competing category: amino acids feeding succinyl-CoA.

Explanation: S-adenosylmethionine donates methyl groups to each process, linking one-carbon metabolism to energy storage, catecholamines, membranes, and gene regulation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: SAM-dependent methylation processes; Uses of S-adenosylmethionine
Source Section: One-Carbon Metabolism > The Activated Methyl Group Cycle, PDF p. 53
Notes: Other methylation reactions also qualify; do not add RNA or protein methylation tiles to the same board without resolving overlap.

Explanation: Classic CBS-deficiency homocystinuria produces this skeletal, ocular, vascular, and neurologic pattern, distinguishing it from Marfan syndrome.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Homocystinuria clinical clues; Classic homocystinuria manifestations
Source Section: One-Carbon Metabolism > Homocystinuria, PDF p. 55
Notes: Downward (inferonasal) lens displacement and the vascular/neuro features distinguish from Marfan. Do not imply every remethylation disorder has all classic CBS features.

Connection Title: Pathogens associated with chronic granulomatous disease
Explanation: NADPH oxidase deficiency impairs the respiratory burst, causing vulnerability to catalase-positive organisms.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: CGD infection associations; Catalase-positive pathogens important in CGD
Source Section: Oxidative Stress > Respiratory (Oxidative) Burst, PDF p. 60
Notes: These four are selected examples, not an exhaustive pathogen list. Competing category: catalase-positive pathogens.

Connection Title: Metabolic consequences of ethanol-driven NADH excess
Explanation: An increased NADH:NAD+ ratio during ethanol metabolism alters lactate handling, reduces glucose production, promotes ketogenesis, and drives triglyceride accumulation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Effects of ethanol-induced NADH excess; Alcohol-related redox imbalance outcomes
Source Section: Oxidative Stress > Ethanol Metabolism, PDF p. 61
Notes: These findings need not occur together or after every alcohol exposure. Competing category: metabolic complications of alcohol exposure (broader).

Connection Title: Glycogen storage diseases with muscle involvement
Connection Type: Shared tissue involvement within a disease family
Explanation: GSD types II, III, IV, and V involve muscle, although the affected muscle types and presentations differ.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Muscle-involving GSDs; GSD types II, III, IV, and V
Source Section: Glycogen > Overview of Glycogen Storage Diseases, PDF p. 69
Notes: Cori (III) and Andersen (IV) overlap PLX-BCH-015 (hepatic group) - do not combine both categories in one puzzle without resolving interchangeable tiles. Do not imply all four are muscle-only or give identical exercise-test results.

Explanation: Failure of hepatic glucose release in GSD I (glucose-6-phosphatase) produces severe fasting hypoglycemia with lactate, lipid, and uric-acid abnormalities.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: GSD I laboratory findings; Von Gierke biochemical signature
Source Section: Glycogen > Von Gierke Disease and Summary, PDF pp. 70, 76
Notes: Cori has milder hypoglycemia with normal lactate and uric acid. Severity varies; do not require every abnormality at every measurement.

Explanation: Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causes lysosomal glycogen storage with characteristic skeletal and cardiac muscle findings, classically in the infantile form.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: GSD II clinical and biopsy clues; Pompe manifestations
Source Section: Glycogen > Pompe Disease, PDF p. 71
Notes: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and macroglossia characterize the infantile phenotype and are less prominent in late-onset disease; retain the infantile qualifier.

Connection Type: Shared disease clinical and laboratory pattern
Explanation: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency impairs muscle glycogen use, producing second wind, exertional muscle injury, an absent lactate rise on the ischemic forearm test, and preserved blood glucose.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: GSD V associations; McArdle exercise and laboratory findings
Source Section: Glycogen > McArdle Disease, PDF p. 74
Notes: A flat lactate response is not exclusive to McArdle; do not use the entry as a testing recommendation. Competing category: other exertional myopathies.

Connection Title: Extrahepatic tissues that can oxidize ketone bodies
Explanation: These tissues can oxidize liver-produced ketone bodies in mitochondria during glucose scarcity; brain ketone use depends on metabolic state and adaptation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Ketone-utilizing extrahepatic tissues; Tissues capable of ketolysis
Source Section: Lipid Metabolism > Ketone Synthesis and Oxidation, PDF p. 95
Notes: The liver cannot use ketones (lacks thiophorase/SCOT); do not include RBCs (no mitochondria). These are not the only ketone-using tissues.

Connection Type: Shared disease presentation and laboratory appearance
Explanation: Type I familial dyslipidemia (LPL or apoC-II deficiency) causes marked chylomicron/triglyceride elevation with these skin, pancreatic, organ, and plasma findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Type I dyslipidemia findings; Familial hyperchylomicronemia clues
Source Section: Lipid Metabolism > Familial Dyslipidemias, PDF p. 89
Notes: Findings do not uniquely prove the inherited enzyme defect. Competing category: chylomicronemia syndrome (familial or acquired).

Connection Type: Shared disease presentation and laboratory pattern
Explanation: Familial type IIa hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor defect) causes high LDL, tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus, and premature atherosclerotic disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Type IIa dyslipidemia findings; Familial hypercholesterolemia associations
Source Section: Lipid Metabolism > Familial Dyslipidemias, PDF p. 89
Notes: Corneal arcus is not diagnostic of inherited disease by itself and must be interpreted with age and the other findings.

Explanation: Trypsin proteolytically activates each pancreatic precursor into an active digestive protease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Trypsin-activated digestive zymogens; Pancreatic protease precursors activated by trypsin
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Protein Digestion and Absorption, PDF p. 103
Notes: Procarboxypeptidase A and B are distinct enzymes, not duplicate aliases. Trypsinogen is itself activated by enteropeptidase (keep off this board); exclude pepsinogen. Competing category: pancreatic digestive zymogens.

Explanation: These signaling molecules and the pigment melanin are downstream of tyrosine metabolism.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tyrosine-derived molecules; Products of tyrosine biosynthesis pathways
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Phenylalanine, Tyrosine, and Catecholamines, PDF p. 105
Notes: Melanin prevents catecholamines from being a valid four-member alternate. Phenylalanine-derived products is acceptable when the tyrosine intermediate is acknowledged. No one-step conversion claim.

Explanation: Phenylalanine accumulation and impaired downstream tyrosine/melanin production cause these findings in untreated PKU.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PKU clinical associations; Phenylketonuria manifestations
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Clinical Implications of Phenylalanine Metabolism, PDF p. 106
Notes: These are untreated-disease findings; a patient treated after newborn screening may not develop them.

Connection Type: Shared disease presentation and laboratory pattern
Explanation: Impaired homogentisate breakdown (homogentisate oxidase deficiency) connects darkening urine, connective-tissue pigmentation, and joint disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Homogentisate oxidase deficiency clues; Alkaptonuria manifestations
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Clinical Implications of Phenylalanine Metabolism, PDF p. 106
Notes: Arthritis develops with age; absence in an infant does not invalidate the association. Black standing urine is distinct from AIP port-wine urine.

Connection Title: Diagnostic clues for maple syrup urine disease
Connection Type: Shared disease presentation and biochemical pattern
Explanation: Deficient branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase causes accumulation of BCAAs and their ketoacids, with characteristic urine odor and neurologic dysfunction.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: MSUD diagnostic findings; Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency clues
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Branched Chain Amino Acids, PDF p. 110
Notes: Infantile dystonia is one possible neurologic manifestation, not universal across MSUD phenotypes.

Explanation: Failure of cystine reabsorption causes urinary cystine accumulation and crystallization; the stone pattern and qualitative test are diagnostic clues.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cystine stone disorder findings; Cystinuria diagnostic associations
Source Section: Protein Metabolism > Cystinuria and Organic Acidemias, PDF p. 109
Notes: The nitroprusside test is not independently specific in all settings; crystal and cystine findings are stronger anchors. Differs from PLX-BCH-003 (transported amino acid identities) - do not co-place.

Connection Type: Shared adverse effect or disease consequence
Explanation: These nutritional, toxic, and medication-related factors disturb heme synthesis and can cause sideroblastic anemia.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Acquired contributors to sideroblastic anemia; Causes of impaired heme synthesis with ring sideroblasts
Source Section: Porphyrias > Heme Synthesis and Heme Synthesis Regulation, PDF pp. 120-121; Vitamins > Vitamin B6, PDF p. 136
Notes: Isoniazid depletes B6, so these two can lie on the same causal chain but remain distinct etiologic tiles. Competing category: impaired heme synthesis.

Explanation: Defective heme production traps iron in erythroid mitochondria, producing this marrow, blood-film, red-cell-size, and iron pattern.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Sideroblastic anemia laboratory and morphology clues; Impaired heme synthesis anemia pattern
Source Section: Porphyrias > Heme Synthesis Regulation and Sideroblastic Anemia, PDF p. 121; Vitamins > Vitamin B6, PDF p. 136
Notes: Source-described pattern, not mandatory criteria: MCV can vary and basophilic stippling is particularly associated with lead. Competing category: lead-associated sideroblastic anemia.

Explanation: These exposures can precipitate attacks in susceptible individuals by inducing ALAS1/CYP demand in the setting of impaired heme precursor processing.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Acute intermittent porphyria attack triggers; Exposures precipitating AIP attacks
Source Section: Porphyrias > Acute Intermittent Porphyria, PDF p. 122
Notes: Tiles include exposures, not only drugs; generic drug enzyme inducers is insufficient. Do not infer that all antiseizure drugs or all sedatives are porphyrinogenic. Competing category: porphyrinogenic exposures.

Connection Type: Shared disease presentation and diagnostic finding
Explanation: Cutaneous porphyrin accumulation causes sun-exposed blistering and skin changes; urine fluoresces pink/coral under a Wood lamp.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PCT cutaneous and urine clues; Porphyria cutanea tarda manifestations
Source Section: Porphyrias > Porphyria Cutanea Tarda, PDF p. 123
Notes: Pink fluorescence requires the Wood lamp context; do not imply pink urine on ordinary inspection. Competing category: pseudoporphyria (lacks the urine finding).

Connection Title: Ocular findings of vitamin A deficiency
Explanation: Vitamin A deficiency impairs rod vision and causes ocular surface injury, producing these classic findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Vitamin A deficiency eye findings; Ocular manifestations of retinol deficiency
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin A, PDF p. 128
Notes: Xerophthalmia can function as an umbrella term encompassing some listed manifestations; these are conventionally taught as separate findings.

Explanation: Chronic vitamin A excess causes hair loss, liver injury, joint symptoms, and intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Chronic hypervitaminosis A manifestations; Chronic retinoid excess findings
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin A, PDF p. 128
Notes: Do not assert every retinoid formulation or dose has an identical toxicity profile. Competing category: retinoid toxicity.

Explanation: Deficient mineralization of growing bone produces these limb, costochondral, and skull findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Rickets skeletal manifestations; Childhood vitamin D deficiency bone findings
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin D, PDF p. 129
Notes: Other causes of rickets also produce these signs, so findings do not uniquely establish a nutritional cause. Do not generalize pediatric skull findings to adult osteomalacia.

Explanation: Thiamine deficiency causes acute and chronic neurocognitive syndromes and neurologic or cardiovascular beriberi.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Vitamin B1 deficiency syndromes; Thiamine deficiency clinical syndromes
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin B1, PDF p. 133
Notes: Wernicke and Korsakoff are related clinical stages. Thiamine deficiency also occurs without alcohol, so alcohol-associated syndromes is less precise.

Connection Type: Shared vitamin depletion or impaired synthesis
Explanation: Inadequate intake, impaired tryptophan-to-niacin conversion (B6), reduced tryptophan absorption (Hartnup), and diversion of tryptophan to serotonin (carcinoid) each reduce niacin availability.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pellagra risk factors; Causes of reduced niacin availability
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin B3, PDF p. 135; Protein Metabolism > Tryptophan, Niacin, and Serotonin, PDF p. 107
Notes: Do not imply every patient with these conditions develops pellagra, or that carcinoid is an amino acid transporter defect. Competing category: pellagra causes.

Explanation: Loss of PLP-dependent functions affects neurotransmitter pathways and heme production and produces characteristic oral findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Pyridoxine deficiency findings; PLP deficiency manifestations
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamin B6, PDF p. 136
Notes: Neuropathy also occurs with B6 excess, but excess does not explain the full deficiency constellation. Competing category: isoniazid-associated B6 depletion.

Connection Type: Shared deficiency-related laboratory and neurologic pattern
Explanation: B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and both homocysteine and methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism, and causes characteristic spinal cord injury.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cobalamin deficiency findings; B12 laboratory and neurologic signature
Source Section: Vitamins > Vitamins B9 and B12, PDF p. 138
Notes: Folate deficiency raises homocysteine but not MMA and lacks the spinal-cord pattern. Neurologic findings can occur without anemia; the four need not be simultaneous.

Explanation: Zinc is a cofactor for each enzyme or family, linking it to peptide processing, acid-base chemistry, phosphate hydrolysis, and DNA synthesis.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Zinc-requiring enzymes; Enzymes with zinc cofactor associations
Source Section: Vitamins > Trace Elements, PDF p. 140
Notes: DNA polymerase is a family-level tile that may need more precise wording for advanced audiences; zinc is not the only metal needed for catalysis (e.g., Mg in polymerases).

Explanation: Zinc deficiency impairs healing and causes hair loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, and altered taste.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Zinc depletion manifestations; Zinc deficiency clinical associations
Source Section: Vitamins > Trace Elements, PDF p. 140
